Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

#9637. From RAG to Riches: The Enterprise Blueprint for Building Production-Grade RAG

I am a Google Product Expert, Google Developer, and global speaker who has mentored tech talent across four continents.

I am a Google Product Expert, Google Developer, and global speaker who has mentored tech talent across four continents.

I am a Google Product Expert, Google Developer, and global speaker who has mentored tech talent across four continents.

Why Naive RAG fails in production (and how to fix it)

While Naive RAG works well for proof of concept, it fails completely in a real world enterprise environment. Below are reasons for this and how you can professionally upgrade your system.

Issue: Basic RAG will take all corporate documents and put them into one large index. This can create a massive security issue. An entry level employee can ask the AI about company salaries or executive emails and it will return the data.

Solution: Implement Document Level Access Control (ACLs). The retrieval system will need to check what the user has permission to view in the corporate environment.

Ingestion – Garbage In = Hallucinations Out

A lot of this happens pre-embedding. Ensure you have identified authoritative sources and owners. Remove duplicates, obsolete and low quality documents. Ensure you retain metadata – source, title, sub heading, page number, date, access control list and version number. Support multiple document types (PDF, DOCX, HTML, tables and images) using structured parsing and OCR. Ensure ingesting is incremental, there is de-dupe in place and there is verifiable deletion. Treating your knowledge base as a product, version your documents and have a plan in place to regularly re-sync.

This often has the biggest impact on the accuracy of your system than your embedding or LLM. Best practice recommendations for production are: Use recursive or structured chunking. Use chunk sizes of 300-512 tokens (with 50-100 tokens or 10-20% overlap) for many enterprise corpora. Ensure you retain structure in your data using parent/child chunking. For technical documents ensure you don’t split code and explanations. For legal/policy ensure clauses aren’t split. Only try semantic/LLM chunking once you have measured baseline performance. Ensure you are trying chunking strategies based on real question sets.

We’ve moved beyond vector search. Using hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse/BM25) will give you gains in your recall and precision. Especially if you have queries with specific IDs, rare terms or jargon. Use hybrid retrieval to gain a larger candidate set. Use metadata filtering for access & freshness. Use cross encoder to rerank your top candidates. You can often get good ROI from adding reranking. This will provide you with meaningful gains to your accuracy with minimal gains to your latency.

Not all queries should be treated the same. Production systems will use categorisation/routing, expansion (HyDE style or multi query), multiple indexes/tools and ‘I don’t know’ scenarios. For complex multi-hop or comparison queries you can use light agent patterns. However this should be done once your retrieval is performing well. Agent patterns can be costly so ensure you’re getting good ROI.

Ensure you use grounded prompts to ensure the LLM only uses information from what is provided in the context. Ask the LLM to cite sources. Ensure citations are structured and check that what is being claimed can be traced back to your retrieved chunks. Ensure you have input/output guardrails, PII and out-of-scope detection. If possible use multiple models. Use cheaper/fast models for simple queries and powerful models for complex synthesis. Ensure you can audit your generation.

You can’t improve what you can’t measure. Use RAGAS or other tools to measure: Context precision/recall Faithfulness Relevance Latency (P95) Citations and user signals. Automate your evaluation using CI/CD. Ensure you have a golden set of real questions. Monitor samples in production using LLM judge and manual checks. Ensure your whole pipeline is instrumented with distributed tracing to help identify where your bad answer is coming from. Often your aims will be to have a faithfulness score above 0.85-0.90, context precision above 0.75-0.80 and latency within acceptable levels. Security/Governance/Multi-tenancy Your RAG system will succeed or fail based on trust. Ensure access to documents/chunks are restricted during retrieval. Multi-tenant, encryption and auditing. Ensure PII is handled carefully. Support deletion. Ensure your knowledge is traceable.

Any existing data vulnerabilities will be amplified in production. So it's essential to get your access controls right early: Implement filtering based on metadata. Ensure users can only see documents they have access to. Scale Often you'll find that having the best infrastructure and caching mechanisms in place will reduce latencies better than using the latest model. Consider: Sharing and replicating your vector indexes. Be mindful of how you shard and replicate your vectors to avoid any latency issues caused by your growing corpus of data. Reduce token costs by implementing semantic caching. Cache popular queries. Use a Multi-model architecture. Consider the cost of having up-to-date data. You'll need to strike the right balance between having to re-index frequently and the latency of your data.

Ensure your solution is built with observability in mind. From day one ensure your solution can handle high volumes of concurrent requests and cold starts. Build your solution RAG is an iterative process. Build your solution in stages.

Stage 1 – Get your basics right : Get your use case specific. Start with one use case and clean data. Build your test set. Build a set of 50 to 100+ questions and answers. Ensure your data is optimised. Ensure your chunking strategy is optimal and your metadata is well tagged.

Stage 2 – Get your solution ready for production. Improve retrieval. Ensure you utilise hybrid search and re-ranking in your solution. Ensure there are security barriers. Ensure you have access restrictions, citations and LLM protections. Ensure your solution has monitoring.

Stage 3 – Optimise Once your basics are in place, add extra complexity. Add query rewriting, hierarchical retrieval, multi-modal capabilities and limited agentic solutions. Business Benefits Having a solid RAG solution in production will give compound benefits: Faster response times from experts. Reduced support tickets. Improved compliance. Ensure knowledge stays within the company should staff leave. A springboard for creating advanced AI agents.

#9634. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

By Meera Joshi, Head of Research and Education, Coinwise Research Circle, Bhopal.

Advance reading plan, prepared 19 November 2026. June 2027 is in the future. CoinMarketCal event dates remain unverified, and the rate examples below are historical—not forecasts. Background reading links are suggested from general knowledge and have not been freshly checked.

Network speed is useful only when we understand what is being counted, what users pay and what happens when something goes wrong.

Learn the network’s building blocks. Start with the introductory sections of the Solana documentation. Focus on accounts, transactions and fees before exploring advanced development.

Read operational evidence. Visit Solana’s status page. Compare a network’s reliability history with its marketing claims. A status page is useful evidence, but not a complete security assessment.

Calendar watch — CoinMarketCal. [CONFIRM] Look for a June 2027 validator-client release or network upgrade. A validator client is the software used by computers helping run the network. Verify whether a listed milestone is a proposal, test release or mainnet deployment, and record its title, date, direct event link and original announcement. The calendar lookup was unavailable during preparation, so no June release is being asserted here. Do not assume a new client is widely adopted merely because it has launched.

Rate watch — CurrencyScoop/CurrencyBeacon. Follow SOL/USD alongside USD/INR. In the historical 11–18 November 2026 comparison, the implied SOL/USD price fell approximately 10.33%. Token performance does not, by itself, prove that network performance improved or deteriorated. [UPDATE] For a June month-end follow-up, compare consistent snapshots for 31 May and 30 June 2027 once available.

Try this: When someone quotes a throughput number, ask whether failed transactions and validator votes are included, over what period it was measured, and how it compares with the transactions users actually want to make. Reading requires no token purchase.

With USD as the base, returned SOL rates were 0.01203438 SOL per USD on 11 November 2026 and 0.01342053 on 18 November 2026. USD per SOL is the reciprocal of each quote; the percentage change is (old_rate / new_rate - 1) * 100. These are provider reference rates, not executable exchange quotes. Confirm current prices, timestamps and event announcements before relying on this plan in June.

#9632. Meet the Writer: Alena Belova on Reputation, AI Search and the Numbers Nobody Publishes

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

Welcome to HackerNoon’s Meet the Writer Interview series, where we learn a bit more about the contributors that have written some of our favorite stories.

My first job, in 2015, was finding out what people really think of things: market research, then reputation analysis for a national lottery brand. Everyone has a view of a lottery. Nobody is neutral. Then I moved to Istanbul and co-founded an e-commerce business selling Turkish goods directly to customers. That is where I learned what I now tell founders: you can be the voice of your company, but the product needs its own accounts, its own email and its own search presence from day one.

Later I worked on a large language model project. From that side you learn two things quickly. An answer is never as fixed as it looks: while a model is still being worked on, the same question can come back noticeably different from one round to the next. And geography matters, just as it always did in search. The same question asked from two countries can return two different pictures of the same company.

That path explains where I am now. I'm a partner at BARS Agency. We build and promote digital products, work on reputation and on how people and companies are presented in AI search. Geometrika started there as a tool we built for ourselves and our clients, to see how AI assistants describe a brand and which sources they lean on, so that strategy could start from data instead of guesses. Exhibo, a global art gallery and culture platform where I'm co-founder and editor-in-chief, asks the same question about culture: which galleries, museums and places become visible online and which quietly drop out.

On paper, these look like different careers. It's one question asked in different rooms: how does something get seen and why do people believe what they see?

I studied art history and I'm studying psychology now, which covers both halves of that question. I lived in Istanbul for several years. These days I live between Doha, Dubai and Egypt.

My latest Top Story asked why a two-hour transfer in the Alps can cost more than the flight that got you there. It belongs to a series I keep coming back to: hidden economics, the prices everyone pays and nobody explains. The newest piece in it is about film rebates in the Middle East. The detail I can't stop thinking about is that a desert now comes with a percentage attached. Every line producer knows the rates by heart. Almost no government in the region publishes what it has actually paid out.

The method doesn't change from piece to piece. Start with a number that should be public. Find out whether it is. If it is, read every row of it.

On HackerNoon it's mostly search, AI and the psychology around them. Somewhere along the way the psychology pieces and the search pieces turned into the same subject. People tend to accept a coherent, confident explanation without checking how it was put together. Memory does it to us: a manager sincerely remembers backing the idea that won. AI answers do it for us: one fluent paragraph, assembled from sources of very different quality, reads as settled fact.

Elsewhere it's culture. At Exhibo I write about art, architecture and the stories attached to objects and places. One pattern keeps coming back: fiction borrows a real place and forgets to give it back. Tatooine is in Tunisia. Agrabah is stitched together from real cities.

The subjects wander. The question underneath doesn't: what is actually going on beneath something everyone takes at face value?

I start with a table. Whatever I want to know, row by row. Half of it usually fills in an afternoon. The piece lives in the cells that refuse to fill.

Then I go to the primary documents, which in this region often means a French PDF, a ministry decree or a press release that is generous with every number except the one you need. When I find a dataset I add it back up against its own totals before I trust a single figure from it.

The research eats the writing. I can spend a week finding out that a number almost never exists in public. That week is invisible in the final piece. Finding out that something isn't there is a finding too. It just takes longer to write down.

The other challenge is restraint. When you've read seven years of a ledger, you want to show the reader every row. The reader wants three.

I want companies to be able to see how AI systems describe them and where that picture comes from, the way they once learned to read their own search results. Most still check it by asking ChatGPT about themselves once and hoping for the best. And what actually moves those answers is rarely what anyone expects. Start a podcast and the assistants often pick it up. I once shared a few of my own photos of desert monasteries. Within weeks the AI version of me had become a cultural heritage contributor and was drifting towards "philanthropist". Nobody has ever complained about that particular error.

I want the same for culture. A serious gallery in Doha or a small museum in Cairo shouldn't disappear from what people find online simply because the information about it was never made easy to find.

Trips planned around exactly one thing I want to see. Lately it's usually a ruin with a desert around it, though it can just as easily be a coastline or a forest. Everything else is allowed to happen on the way, as long as there's European coffee somewhere on the route.

And when the list runs out, I go out into the desert just to look at nothing for an hour. It is the only place where my phone and I agree to ignore each other.

Languages. Spanish, Arabic and, less gracefully, Turkish. Spanish feels familiar, at least in its logic. Arabic and Turkish don't. Many Arabic words are built from three-consonant roots, so one root gives you a writer, a book and an office. In Turkish a whole sentence can be a single word thirty letters long. Both break my brain a little.

Translators and AI do fine with a menu. Face to face, they still get lost. So I'm doing it the long way.

And art, which stopped being a hobby the day it became a job. I will still talk Monet and Manet with anyone who confuses them.

First, an experiment I've wanted to run for a while: asking every major AI assistant who I am, then tracing the wrong answers back to where they came from, when they came from anywhere at all. A machine's idea of you is assembled from places you have forgotten you ever wrote.

Then more hidden economics: who pays for a free museum. The British Museum opened free in 1759, on a collection a public lottery had helped pay for. In 2026 the Louvre and the Grand Egyptian Museum both raised their prices. Someone always pays. The question is who. And whether they know it.

Where else would a story about airport transfers in the Alps sit next to one about falling in love with chatbots? I've stopped asking which of them is the tech story.

If you ever go looking for a number and it isn't there, write that down. The absence is usually the story.

Rita Sheth on Solopreneurship, AI and Bias in Tech

#9630. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

#9629. How to Automate Income Verification From Pay Stubs, W-2s, and Bank Statements

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at unsiloed.ai

By Aman Mishra. Originally published on Unsiloed AI.

A lender or landlord who wants to know what someone earns usually gets three kinds of paperwork. A pay stub covers one pay period. A W-2 covers last year. A bank statement shows what actually arrived in the account. Each one tells part of the story, and the useful question is whether the parts agree. Answering that by hand means reading figures off five or six pages and doing arithmetic across them, which is slow and easy to get wrong.

We use the Unsiloed extraction API to pull the handful of figures each check needs, each with a confidence score and the exact spot on the page it came from. Then we use Python to compare the documents and hand a person only the parts that don't agree. The guide below takes that approach through one applicant's file, five documents that pass a page-by-page read and fail a cross-check.

Income verification is checking evidence of what someone earns. Automating it means software reads that evidence, compares the figures, and leaves a person only the exceptions. Some services skip the paperwork and connect to payroll or bank accounts directly. This guide covers the other route, where the applicant uploads documents and each one answers a different question.

If the documents arrive in one mixed PDF, classify and separate its pages first. The rest of this guide takes one applicant's file through the four steps.

Elian Voss works for Ternvale Fabrication LLC and banks with Larkmere Bank. The file has two monthly pay stubs, last year's W-2 and two months of bank statements.

Read one page at a time, nothing stands out. The name matches everywhere. Each stub shows $6,000 of gross pay, the figure before deductions, and $4,500 of net pay, the figure that goes to the bank, paid by direct deposit to the account ending 4826. The bank statements are for that same account, and last year's W-2 reports $66,000.

Two things are hiding in these documents. One looks like a problem and isn't. The other looks fine and is a problem. Both only show up when the documents are compared.

A schema tells the API which fields to return and what type each one is. We ask for very little, because every extra field is one more value someone might need to review. The pay stub guide, W-2 form guide and bank statement guide cover extracting each document in full.

The pay stub fields include federal taxable wages, the earnings federal income tax is calculated on. That field turns out to matter more than gross pay.

We send each PDF to the extraction endpoint with its schema and poll until the job finishes. model is set to gamma, which reads these forms reliably, and enable_citations asks for the location of every value.

Every value comes back with two scores and a citation. Here is Box 1 from the W-2.

The extraction_score is the API's confidence in the value itself. The grounding_score is its confidence that it found the value at the cited spot. Both run from zero to one. The citation gives the page and a bounding box, the rectangle on the page where the value sits. That rectangle is what lets every check below point a reviewer to the exact figure behind it.

None of the documents can be verified alone, so each check takes a few fields from two or three of them and compares them.

Each check below is a sketch written against the docs dictionary from the previous step. A production system would add its own handling for low scores and missing values, which we come back to at the end.

Every document should name the same person and the same employer. We lowercase the names and strip punctuation before comparing, which handles "ELIAN VOSS" on the bank statement.

The employer is harder. On the bank statement, the paycheck shows up as TERNVALE FAB PAYROLL PPD, the bank's shorthand for a payroll deposit from Ternvale Fabrication. No string cleanup turns that into "Ternvale Fabrication LLC". Fuzzy matching might, but it might also match a deposit that isn't pay. A small table of descriptions a person has already confirmed is safer, and it grows as reviewers approve new ones.

The September stub shows $6,000 gross pay a month. Multiply by twelve, the usual way to annualize a stub, and the applicant earns $72,000 a year. The W-2 for last year says $66,000 in Box 1. A naive check would flag a $6,000 gap and conclude the stubs overstate the income.

The answer is on the stub itself. Each month, $500 goes into a traditional 401(k), a workplace retirement plan paid into before income tax. The IRS instructions for Box 1 leave those contributions out. So the stub figure to hold against Box 1 is federal taxable wages. $5,500 of taxable pay a month is $66,000 a year, which matches the W-2 exactly.

The year-to-date figure, the running total since January 1, gives a second view of the same year. September's stub shows $49,500 of taxable pay over nine payments, which also projects to $66,000.

These figures match to the dollar because the salary and contribution didn't change between years. With raises, bonuses, hourly pay or a midyear start, compare within a tolerance and send larger gaps to a person with both cited figures.

Each stub says $4,500 went by direct deposit to the account ending 4826. For each stub, we look for a payroll deposit of the same amount within three days of the pay date.

Run against the five documents, the checks print this.

The names agree, and once taxable wages are compared like for like, so does the income. The gap that looked like a problem was a 401(k) contribution. The month that looked fine is the one to worry about. September's paycheck arrived on September 30. The August statement for account 4826 shows rent, groceries, a utility bill and a card payment, and no deposits at all.

The August paycheck is the one exception, and the output says where to look, so a reviewer opens the August stub and the August statement instead of rereading all five documents. There are ordinary explanations, such as a changed account, a delayed payroll run or a stub that doesn't match what was paid. Deciding which applies is a job for a person.

Values with scores below your cutoff, and fields that come back null, are exceptions too, and they go to a person before any comparison runs. The confidence score thresholds guide covers choosing a cutoff for each field.

The same pattern covers whatever else your team checks, such as a second employer or an employment letter. Extract the few fields the check needs, compare them across documents, and keep the citations so every flag points back to the page that raised it. What the loan officer or leasing agent gets is a short list of places where the paperwork disagrees, with the decision still theirs.

#9627. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9625. The Transaction Only Covers Your Database. The Provider Key Is What Saves You

Two readers asked me the same question from opposite sides last week, and I have been running it ever since. itsvicmoreno asked it on my piece about claiming a delivery once: the processed-keys table stops the second copy, but what if the receiver crashes between writing the key and charging the card? sunnatulla_dev asked the matching half on the other piece: he had already tried it in his own head, one crash, two attempts, zero charges: the key written, the retry refused as a duplicate, and nothing ever charged.

Both of them were right to worry. A key and a charge are two separate writes, and a crash can land between them. Which order breaks first, and what actually saves you? I crashed the receiver on purpose, in both orders, against four different shapes, with the same $29 payment for the same order, and counted the charges from the receiver's own tables. The results are clear, and one of them made me change my mind about a fix I used to recommend without thinking.

The first crash is the one sunnatulla_dev described. The receiver writes the key, then dies before the charge. The sender sees the connection drop and tries again. The retry finds the key already in the table and gets a polite 200 duplicate. Nothing charges. Ever.

My run: 2 attempts, 0 charges. Exactly his shape, down to the numbers. The customer is never charged, the order sits unpaid, and nobody gets an error. The system looks healthy from every angle except the one that matters: no money moved. A duplicate refusal is only correct if the first attempt actually did the work, and here it did not. The key is a promise that the charge happened, and the crash broke the promise.

This is the quiet failure, and I think it is the one people underestimate. A double charge shows up in a bank statement and somebody shouts. A lost charge shows up weeks later, in a report, as revenue that never arrived, and by then nobody remembers the crash.

Now flip the order. The receiver charges first, then dies before writing the key. The retry finds no key, so it charges again. Same $29, same order, second charge.

My run: 2 attempts, 2 charges. $58 for a $29 order. This is the order that breaks first, and itsvicmoreno's question bet exactly that: the charge lands and the key never does. The retry has nothing to check, because the only record of the first charge lives at the provider, and this receiver never asks the provider anything.

So both orders are broken, in opposite directions. Key first loses the payment. Charge first doubles it. If you have to pick a failure, pick the lost one — at least nobody's card was charged twice. But picking a failure is not a design. The fix has to cover both orders, not one.

The first fix people reach for is the obvious one: put the key and the charge in one transaction, so they commit together or roll back together. I ran it. Crash before the commit, the whole thing rolls back, the retry charges exactly once. 2 attempts, 1 charge. It works.

But it works only inside your own database. The transaction covers the key and your local record of the charge. The charge itself happens at the provider, outside your database, outside your transaction, outside everything you can roll back. If the crash lands between the provider's charge and your mark-done, the transaction has nothing to say about it. The provider took the money. Your database says processing. The retry has to decide, and the transaction cannot decide for it.

I used to describe the single transaction as the answer to this problem. It is not the answer. It is a good answer to a smaller problem: keeping your own records consistent. The money lives somewhere else, and the fix has to reach there.

The second fix is a status column with a lease. The key goes in as processing, with a time limit. A retry while the lease is alive gets a 409 and waits. After the lease expires, the row can be reclaimed and the charge retried. A crashed holder stops holding the row, eventually.

sunnatulla_dev ran this shape in his own test with a 30 second lease: the copy in flight got a 409, the crashed one got a 409, then it was reclaimed at 60 seconds, one charge each. My job was to check that number, and to set the lease from something real instead of 30 seconds picked out of the air.

So I measured first. One hundred real charge calls through the receiver, and I took the p99, the time almost every healthy call finishes inside. Run 1: p99 1.89 seconds, so the lease was 2.39 seconds. Run 2: p99 0.96 seconds, lease 1.46 seconds. The p99 moved between runs because handler time on this small machine includes scheduling stalls; run 1 even caught a 5.48 second stall. That is the point of measuring: the lease has to beat the longest a healthy handler can actually run on the machine it runs on, stalls included, plus slack. A lease picked from a round number cannot know that.

Then I crashed the lease arm and retried every half second. Run 1: three 409s, reclaimed 3.21 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Run 2: two 409s, reclaimed 2.12 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Not 60 seconds. The reclaim lands one retry after the lease expires, so the honest number is the lease plus your retry gap. His 60 seconds came from his 30 second lease plus his retry rhythm, not from the mechanism. With a lease set from p99, the crashed row is reclaimable roughly one lease after the crash, about two to three seconds here.

One more detail that matters: while the charge runs, the handler renews the lease, every third of a lease. Without that, a slow-but-alive charge gets reclaimed mid-flight and charges twice, which is the exact failure the lease was supposed to prevent. A lease without renewal is a timer that punishes the slow and rewards the dead.

The third fix is the one itsvicmoreno pointed at. Insert the key as processing, pass that same key to the provider as its idempotency key, then mark it done. A retry that finds processing does not charge again. It asks the provider: did this key already charge? If yes, mark it done and stop.

I crashed this shape after the provider charge, before the mark-done. 2 attempts, 1 provider charge, 1 local charge. The retry asked, the provider said already charged, nothing charged twice. Then I ran it in the charge-first order too: provider charge first, local key still pending, crash, retry, and the retry asked the provider first, before touching the local key table. Same result: 1 provider charge. It is the only shape in the test that stays at exactly one charge in both orders, including the window the transaction cannot see.

That is my claim, and I expect people to argue with it: the single transaction is the wrong place to put your trust, because the money does not live in your database. The status column with a measured lease is good and honest, and I would keep it as the backstop. But the thing that actually saves you from a crash between the key and the charge is the provider's own idempotency key, the same key on both sides, with the retry asking instead of charging. Everything else is bookkeeping about a charge that already happened somewhere else.

Have you ever been charged twice for one order, or had a payment quietly never go through after a crash? Which side did it break on, and what did the retry do: ask first, or charge first? I would like to hear what it was, because the retry is where the money is decided, and most of us never look at it until it has already decided wrong.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

#9624. We Started With Four Open Agent CLI Questions. We Ended With Two Real Wins.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is the Tier-1 part of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

At one point, the entire Tier-1 CLI section of the field test was still unresolved.

That was the honest state. Claude Code had not run live yet. Codex had not run live yet. Cursor and Gemini had not been closed out either. If I had stopped there, the report would have been accurate but incomplete.

So I kept going case by case, with one rule: do not claim a harness until it runs with evidence on this box.

That persistence changed the release in a meaningful way. Claude Code and Codex both went live. Cursor and Gemini both got real investigations and honest noes. We shipped the two we could prove and left the other two out.

The Tier-1 set in the plan was four CLIs: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Gemini. Early in the sweep, none of them belonged in a green release note. The report had to say that plainly.

This is where the field-test discipline mattered. A case was only real if it ran through the actual harness and left evidence behind: verdict, assertions, transcripts, audit trail, and captured LLM traffic. If it did not, it stayed unproven.

That kept me from turning "probably works" into "supported."

Claude Code was the first real win, and it took more than a config toggle. The working harness is in scripts/fieldtest/t1_claude.sh, with the hook entrypoint in t1_evaluate.py and the shared policy in t1_policy.yaml.

Once that wiring was real, the case passed live: a read executed, a prod write escalated without creating the side-effect file, a destructive command was denied, and the audit trail recorded all three decisions. Six request/response pairs were captured.

Codex needed a different investigation. Its harness lives in scripts/fieldtest/t1_codex.sh.

The key findings were different from Claude's:

Codex also forced a more honest test shape. Headless Codex does not expose a pausable per-call approval hook like Claude. So the case proves what the surface actually supports: allow executes, deny holds and replans, plus pre-execution parity against the same in-process policy engine. That is a real pass, just not the same kind of pass as Claude.

The result was still strong: live run, captured traffic, parity audit trail, destructive command blocked, target directory intact.

Gemini was not a hand-wave. The local install worked. gemini gemma setup brought up a local server. But the CLI's main loop still could not run locally because the local gemma route is classifier-only and the CLI hits an OAuth tier gate before any model routing. That is all documented in the report and backed by the bundle-source read plus the parity stand-in that did run.

Cursor was a different kind of limitation. There is no supported headless surface on this box for the permissions.json flow. Cursor is a GUI IDE, and without a reproducible, evidence-capturing path, there was no honest live case to claim.

Those are not failures to hide. They are useful boundaries. They tell the release exactly what it supports today and what would need to change for the other two to re-enter scope.

The encouraging part of this story is not "we only got two." It is that we started with four question marks and finished with two live integrations, two investigated boundaries, and a release note I can defend line by line.

Have you had a release where the strongest part of the story was not the things that passed, but the things you proved carefully enough to leave out?

#9622. Your AI Agents Will Be Attacked. Red-Team Them First

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

By Pramin Pradeep, Co-founder & CEO, BotGauge AI

For most of the last few years, my job was making software prove it works. At BotGauge, we built autonomous QA that tested our customers' apps before every release. Then those same customers started shipping AI agents, and the old playbook stopped being enough.

A test suite asks one question: does this do what it should? An agent needs a second one: what will it do when someone wants it to misbehave? That second question is red teaming. It's why we launched our agent red-teaming platform on October 28, 2026 and the developer community noticed: it finished #3 Product of the Day on Product Hunt.

Red teaming isn't new. It started as military war-gaming, became a staple of security teams paid to break in, and with LLMs turned into jailbreaking chatbots.

Agents raise the stakes because they act. They call tools, read inboxes, write to databases and hand tasks to other agents. A bad chatbot answer is embarrassing. A bad agent action is an incident.

And adoption is outrunning testing. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. Yet most teams I talk to test agents like APIs: happy paths, a few edge cases, a vibe check. None of that simulates an adversary.

OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top risk for LLM applications, but for agents it's only the front door. Here's what we see:

•       Indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in a web page, PDF, email or support ticket the agent reads mid-task.

•       Tool misuse: tricking the agent into calling a legitimate tool with harmful arguments, like a refund, a delete or an outbound email.

•       Data exfiltration: coaxing the agent into leaking customer data, system prompts or credentials through its outputs or tool calls.

•       Goal hijacking: slow, multi-turn manipulation that drifts the agent away from its task without tripping any single-message filter.

•       Multi-agent cascades: one compromised agent passing poisoned context to others that trust it by default.

Our autonomous QA product had paying customers and a working business. But functional testing was maturing fast, and the problem our customers kept raising wasn't "does it work?" It was "can I trust it in production?"

So we rebuilt BotGauge as an Agent Control Plane, and made one calls early:

●      Red teaming at the core, not a checkbox. Observability tells you what happened. Red teaming tells you what could happen, before a user or attacker finds it.

The goal is simple: attack your agent the way an adversary would, every time it changes, and show you exactly where it broke.

•       200+ custom attack strategies spanning injection, tool misuse, exfiltration, goal hijacking and jailbreaks, run against your real agent, not a sandboxed copy of the model.

•       Full tracing: every failed attack links to its trace, so you see which input, which step and which tool call went wrong.

•       Evals that persist: results are scored and compared across releases, so a fix doesn't quietly regress next sprint.

•       Fits your stack: it sits on top of runtimes like LangGraph and AWS Bedrock AgentCore instead of replacing them.

Your agents will be attacked. Regulators are already moving: NIST's AI risk guidance and the EU AI Act both call for adversarial testing. The only real question is who finds the holes first, your team or someone else. I'd rather it be you.

Pramin Pradeep is co-founder and CEO of BotGauge AI, an Agent Control Plane for testing, observing and governing AI agents in production. BotGauge is backed by Surface Ventures, IA Seed Ventures and Saka Ventures. *Sources

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9620. Who controls you more: your government or your feed?

There are two ways to change what millions of people think and do.

The first is old and loud. A government switches off the internet. In 2024, according to Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition, governments and other actors imposed 296 internet shutdowns in 54 countries, the worst year on record (Access Now, 2025). Everyone notices. People complain, find a VPN, wait, and remember.

The second is new and quiet. A ranking system decides which of a thousand posts you see first. Nobody switches anything off. In 2014, researchers published an experiment in which Facebook adjusted the emotional content of the News Feed for 689,003 users for one week, and those users' own posts shifted slightly in the same emotional direction (Kramer, Guillory & Hancock, PNAS 2014). Almost nobody noticed. That was the point.

So here is the question I want to put on the table: which of these two has more power over your daily life?

States still hold the hardest kinds of power: police, prisons, borders, currency, and, increasingly, the kill switch for the network itself. A feed can nudge your mood; a government can take your phone at a checkpoint. When the internet goes dark in a conflict zone, no algorithm brings it back.

Anyone who says "governments do not matter anymore, only platforms do" has probably never lived through a shutdown.

But a shutdown is visible, and visible power produces resistance. Ranking systems work differently:

Power that you invite into your pocket and thank for its convenience is a very different kind of power.

I trained as a control engineer, and I keep seeing society as a feedback loop. I wrote about this in Arabic as a society without an integral term: a hotel shower where the water arrives late, so you keep correcting too hard, swinging between burning and freezing.

Feeds are tuned for exactly that swing: react fast, react strongly, forget, react again. The missing piece in that loop, what engineers call the integral term, is simply memory: the slow accumulation of what actually happened, that stops the system from overreacting to every new signal.

Both governments and algorithms are easier to resist for people with memory: people who read long things, keep notes, remember last month's outrage before joining this week's.

The Amish are often described as people who reject technology. They did not reject the telephone. As sociologist Donald Kraybill described, many communities kept it out of the house, in a shared booth at the end of the road. They took the tool and changed its place. I wrote about that in how to use technology without it using you.

That is the most realistic defense most of us have, against either kind of control:

I explore the quieter kind of control at more length in an open research paper, in Arabic: Moral Desertification and Liquid Knowledge in the Algorithmic Age. It asks what happens to how values are learned when the feed, not the family or the school, decides what a child sees next.

I'm Saifuddin Ahmed, a control engineer turned software builder and the founder of Ishraqa Daily, a community on Google Play, the App Store and the Microsoft Store that turns knowledge into impact: developer clubs where people build open-source projects with mentors, languages, reading and listening together, and scholarships and opportunities. I also built Rafu and founded OtwoX Digital Solutions. More of my work is at saifuddin.dev and on LinkedIn.

I drafted this piece with an AI writing assistant. The ideas come from my own essays and experience, and the questions are the ones I am still thinking about.

#9617. Preventing double-booked meeting rooms in Laravel: setup buffers, pending holds and all-or-nothing recurring series

Ejtma is a meeting room booking system used by companies in Saudi Arabia. A common question in any booking system is "why can't I book this room? It looks free." In Ejtma the answer is usually one of three rules: setup time, a booking that waits for approval, or one meeting in a weekly series. This post shows how we check conflicts and how each rule works.

A booking has the time the user picked (start_at, end_at) and the time the room is actually busy (actual_start_at, actual_end_at).

The difference comes from services. A booking can request services such as catering. Each service has preparing and cleaning minutes, and the room is blocked for those minutes too:

A 10:00 to 11:00 meeting with catering that needs 20 minutes to set up and 30 to clear blocks the room from 09:40 to 11:30. The calendar shows 10:00 to 11:00, because that is the meeting. Conflict checks use the actual times, because that is when the room is busy.

All conflict queries use one scope. It lists the four ways two ranges can overlap:

The ASCII comments make code review easy. The strict > and < in the last two cases matter: a meeting that ends at 11:00 does not conflict with one that starts at 11:00. Back-to-back bookings are normal and must work.

If you write this from scratch, the short form gives the same result for normal ranges: start < :end AND end > :start.

Some bookings need approval in up to three parts: the time, the requested services, and a parking request. While a booking waits, it still blocks the room:

The other choice is "first approved wins". With that rule, two people book the same room, both wait two days, one gets approved, and the other learns late that the room is gone. Holding the slot means the second person sees the conflict at once and picks another time.

The check runs again when an approver accepts a booking. Data can change between the request and the approval, and the approver should not publish a conflict.

A published booking can be changed. The change creates a new version that waits for approval, and the published version stays on the calendar until then. Without care, the new version conflicts with its own parent. The check excludes the record and every version of the same booking:

A weekly meeting for three months has about 13 occurrences. If one of them conflicts, we reject the whole series and name the date:

Creating 12 of 13 meetings and skipping one sounds friendly. But a skipped week is easy to miss in a warning, and the team then arrives at a room that is taken. A clear rejection with the date lets the organizer move that one week or pick another room.

Each occurrence is also checked against room maintenance windows, with the same buffers.

When a single booking conflicts, the booking form asks for suggestions in this order:

Every suggestion is checked against bookings and maintenance windows before it is shown.

#9615. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.
